Lessons.Title: Writing and Solving Inequalities in One Variable
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: create and solve contextual one-variable inequalities, check assumptions and use algebraic structure to interpret signs and all-real solution sets. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L20, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/20/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Addressing HSA-CED.A.1, HSA-CED.A.3 and HSA-REI.B.3.

Original numbers for a fictional rehearsal dinner: food costs $5.29 per pound, two water bottles cost $2.49 each, and total budget is at most $60. Let x≥0 pounds of food. Constraint 5.29x+2(2.49)≤60. Subtract 4.98: 5.29x≤55.02; divide positive 5.29 to obtain x≤55.02/5.29≈10.40076. If food is sold to the nearest tenth-pound, maximum allowed is 10.4 pounds.

Structure warm-up: 0.5x>10x leads −9.5x>0, so x<0; for negative values multiplying by 0.5 gives a number less negative than multiplying by 10. Conversely, x<x+5 is true for every real x because subtracting x gives 0<5. No invented artificial endpoint should be added.

Student task: solve dinner constraint, check x=10.4 versus x=10.5, explain whether food can be fractionally purchased, and classify structural inequalities with zero, negative and positive values. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 max): correct translation, algebra and inequality direction, boundary/domain interpretation, and reasoned structural checks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Budget with fixed cost
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fixed charge plus a variable expense can be bounded by a total budget.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Subtract fixed charges before dividing by positive rate.

KeyConcepts.Title: Negative factor order
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplication or division by a negative number reverses < and >.

KeyConcepts.Title: Always-true inequality
KeyConcepts.Definition: Some inequalities hold over all real values.

WorkedExamples.Title: Solve a dinner budget
WorkedExamples.Question: Maximum food weight with $5.29/lb, $4.98 bottles and $60 budget.
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: If purchased to one decimal place, choose 10.4 pounds.
WorkedExamples.Answer: x≤55.02/5.29 pounds; maximum 10.4 to the nearest tenth-pound.
WorkedExamples.Check: 10.5 pounds would cost $60.525 and exceed budget.

WorkedExamples.Title: Use structure with negative x
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve 0.5x>10x.
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: Divide by negative −9.5 and reverse sign.
Check x=−2 gives −1>−20, true; x=2 gives 1>20 false.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original inequality checked on both sides of zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find all-real solution range
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve x<x+5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: This is true independent of x.
Therefore every real x solves the original inequality.
WorkedExamples.Check: Try negative, zero and positive values; all satisfy.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An increased purchase amount can exceed budget.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check rounded values in original total cost.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reversing inequality even when dividing by a positive factor

SummaryPoints: Translate spending context and fixed charges before solving.
Strict and inclusive boundaries must match the text and units.
An inequality may have an interval, all real solutions or none.
Teacher evaluates assumptions and mathematical reasoning.
